title: REV Control Hub & Expansion Hub: FTC Control Architecture
description: Port breakdown, 12V power distribution, RS-485 communication, motor ports and safe I2C/Digital/Analog wiring for FTC robots.
body: The REV Robotics Control Hub (REV-31-1595) integrates an Android computing platform, dual-band Wi-Fi, and a dedicated IO controller into an integrated FTC brain. The REV Robotics Expansion Hub (REV-31-1153) mirrors the exact same physical and electrical IO interface while delegating computation to the Control Hub through an RS-485 serial bus or to a legacy Android smartphone via USB. Both units operate on 12V nominal DC power supplied by approved NiMH battery packs, with an active input window of 8V to 12V and an absolute non-operating ceiling of 15V. Both hub variants provide identical peripheral port layouts. The table below outlines connectivity specs and channel limits. | Port Bank | Quantity Per Hub | Connector Standard | Technical Specifications and Limits | |---|---:|---|---| | DC Motor | 4 | JST-VH (2-Pin) | H-bridge power stage, 10A continuous per channel, 20A peak current trip, auto thermal shutdown | | Motor Encoder | 4 | JST-PH (4-Pin) | Quadrature incremental encoder inputs (A/B), 3.3V logic level, 500mA combined sensor rail | | Servo Output | 6 | 0.1-inch Header (3-Pin) | 5V PWM signal (500–2500 µs), 2A max per paired port cluster (0-1, 2-3, 4-5), 5A total hub cap | | Analog Inputs | 4 | JST-PH (4-Pin) | 2 channels per port, 0–5.0V input measurement range, 3.3V auxiliary sensor power pin | | Digital IO | 8 | JST-PH (4-Pin) | 2 digital channels per connector, 3.3V logic, configurable as input/output, 1A max total rail | | I²C Busses | 4 | JST-PH (4-Pin) | 4 independent I²C busses, 100 kHz standard or 400 kHz fast mode, 3.3V rail, 2.49 kΩ pull-ups | | RS-485 Bus | 2 | JST-PH (3-Pin) | Differential serial link for daisy-chaining Expansion Hub to Control Hub | | Aux 5V Power | 2 | 0.1-inch Header | Regulated 5V output for external coprocessors or active indicator LEDs, shared 5A pool | Incorrect wiring into JST-PH ports is the primary source of board-level damage. All REV 4-pin sensor ports follow a strict ordering convention: Ground, 3.3V Power, Signal 1, and Signal 2. Pin 1: Ground (Black / Brown) ──── GND reference common Pin 2: VCC Power (Red) ──── +3.3V DC (or +5V via Level Shifter) Pin 3: Signal Channel 0 / SDA ──── Digital IO 0 / Analog In 0 / I2C SDA / Encoder A Pin 4: Signal Channel 1 / SCL ──── Digital IO 1 / Analog In 1 / I2C SCL / Encoder B To bridge the primary Control Hub and an Expansion Hub: Connect an approved 3-pin JST-PH cable between the RS485 ports on both devices. Do not route this line into UART ports. Bridge power by connecting an XT30 male-to-female daisy chain cable from the second XT30 battery port on the Control Hub directly to the Expansion Hub battery input. Configure unique hub addresses within the FTC Driver Station software to prevent bus arbitration collisions. System electrical stability depends on aggregate stall current draw. When 4 drive motors stall simultaneously during rapid directional changes, instantaneous current spikes: I_{peak} = SUM_{m=1}^{n} I_{stall, m} + SUM_{s=1}^{k} I_{servo, s} + I_{electronics} For 4 NeveRest or goBILDA 5202/5203 motors with stall currents around 9.2A each, peak theoretical load exceeds 36A. Internal resistance in wiring, switch contacts, and battery pack causes supply rail droop: V_{drop} = I_{total} * (R_{battery} + R_{wiring} + R_{switch}) If voltage at the Control Hub input pins drops below 8.0V for more than 50 milliseconds, the internal microcontroller risks brownout reboots. To prevent brownouts: Keep main power leads short and constructed with minimum 16 AWG or recommended 14 AWG silicone wire. Inspect XT30 prongs regularly; spread pins slightly if loose mating occurs. Monitor live telemetry via VoltageSensor in autonomous and teleop modes. // Hardware map voltage telemetry check VoltageSensor batterySensor = hardwareMap.voltageSensor.iterator().next(); telemetry.addData("Battery Voltage", "%.2f V", batterySensor.getVoltage()); if (batterySensor.getVoltage() < 10.5) { telemetry.addLine("WARNING: Battery low. Swap pack before match start."); } Verify polarity across XT30 and battery connectors before engaging main power switch. Validate that all 5V sensors running into I²C ports pass through a REV Logic Level Converter (REV-31-1389). Ensure motor encoder channel numbers correspond precisely to the motor power output indices in software configuration. Confirm Expansion Hub LED pulses steady blue or green, verifying active RS-485 packet sync with the Control Hub.

title: Planetary Gearmotors & Smart Servos: Torque vs. Speed Selection
description: Comparing gear ratios for REV UltraPlanetary and goBILDA Yellow Jacket, arm torque calculations, and servo burnout protection.
body: Electromechanical actuation in FIRST Tech Challenge centers around 12V DC brushed gearmotors and 5V pulse-width modulated (PWM) servomotors. Achieving rapid mechanical cycles and precise autonomous repeatability requires a rigorous understanding of planetary reduction ratios, torque-speed curves, encoder resolution, and servo electrical rail constraints. Modern FTC mechanisms leverage high-performance permanent magnet DC motors paired with planetary gearheads and integrated Hall-effect quadrature encoders. | Motor Family | Manufacturer | Nominal Voltage | Bare Motor Free Speed | Representative Gear Ratios | Encoder Architecture | |---|---|---:|---:|---|---| | Yellow Jacket 5202/5203 | goBILDA | 12V DC | 6,000 RPM | 3.7:1, 5.2:1, 13.7:1, 19.2:1, 26.9:1 | Dual-channel Hall (28 CPR base shaft) | | HD Hex Motor | REV Robotics | 12V DC | 6,000 RPM | UltraPlanetary modular cartridges (3:1, 4:1, 5:1) | Dual-channel Hall (28 CPR base shaft) | | Core Hex Motor | REV Robotics | 12V DC | 6,000 RPM | 72:1 integrated gearbox, 5mm hex bore | Dual-channel Hall (288 CPR output shaft) | | NeveRest Classic / Orbital | AndyMark | 12V DC | 6,600 RPM | 3.7:1, 19.2:1, 40:1, 60:1 spur/orbital | Optical or magnetic Hall (7 or 28 CPR) | A permanent magnet DC motor produces an output torque tau that varies linearly with its rotational angular velocity omega : tau(omega) = tau_{stall} (1 - (omega / omega_{free)}) The mechanical power output P_mech delivered to the output shaft peaks at half of the free speed: P_{mech}(omega) = tau(omega) * omega When coupling the motor to a planetary gearbox characterized by gear ratio G ( G > 1 ) and mechanical transmission efficiency eta (typically 0.80 le eta le 0.90 across multi-stage planetary assemblies): tau_{out} = tau_{motor} * G * eta omega_{out} = frac{omega_{motor}}{G} Encoder resolution measured at the final gearbox output shaft depends directly on the base pulse generation rate and the reduction ratio: CPR_{out} = CPR_{base} * G For example, a goBILDA 5202 series motor with a 19.2:1 planetary stage and a 28 CPR base Hall sensor yields: CPR_{out} = 28 * 19.2 = 537.6 counts per revolution The REV Control Hub and Expansion Hub isolate motor drive power from low-voltage encoder signal logic across distinct port types: Motor Power Port (JST-VH 2-Pin): High-current delivery up to 10A continuous / 20A peak trip. Reversing pin polarity reverses motor direction. Encoder Port (JST-PH 4-Pin): Pin 1 (Black/Brown): System Ground (GND) Pin 2 (Red): Regulated +3.3V DC logic supply Pin 3 (Yellow): Quadrature Channel A signal line Pin 4 (White/Blue): Quadrature Channel B signal line [Hub Motor Port: JST-VH] Pin 1 (+) ──────── Motor Terminal (+) Pin 2 (-) ──────── Motor Terminal (-) [Hub Encoder Port: JST-PH] Pin 1: GND ────── Encoder Sensor Ground Pin 2: 3.3V ───── Encoder Logic Supply (+3.3V) Pin 3: Ch A ───── Hall Sensor Phase A Pin 4: Ch B ───── Hall Sensor Phase B Standard servos decode pulse-width modulation signals dispatched at a nominal frequency of 50 Hz (20 ms period). The pulse duration dictates target angular orientation or rotational speed: Pulse Duration Bounds: Standard FTC range spans 500,mus (minimum angle, 0^circ ) to 2500,mus (maximum angle, typically 180^circ to 300^circ ). Connector Pinout (3-Pin 0.1" Header): Pin 1 (Brown/Black): Ground Pin 2 (Red): +5V DC Supply Rail Pin 3 (Orange/White): PWM Control Signal | Servo Class | Operating Modes | Common Subsystem Applications | Stall Current Considerations | |---|---|---|---| | REV Smart Robot Servo (SRS) | Angular (180°/270°) & Continuous Rotation | Gripper pinch, dust flap deploy, intake feed | 2.0A stall limit at 5V | | goBILDA Dual Mode Servo | Standard (300°) & Continuous Rotation | Virtual four-bar wrists, linkage triggers | 2.5A peak stall demand | | Axon Mini / Max Servo | Brushless core, programmatic travel angles | High-speed coaxial swerve, rapid intakes | 3.5A – 4.0A peak current draw | Electrical Power Rail Advisory: Hub internal 5V servo regulators deliver 2A shared between each port pair (ports 0-1, 2-3, 4-5) with a maximum hub-wide cap of 5A. When high-torque mechanisms bind or multiple brushless servos actuate simultaneously, install an external REV Servo Power Module (REV-11-1144) wired directly to 12V battery power to supply up to 15A of clean 6V power. The following FTC SDK routine illustrates how to configure an elevator motor with closed-loop positional targeting and active zero-power braking alongside a calibrated servo gripper: package org.firstinspires.ftc.teamcode; import com.qualcomm.robotcore.eventloop.opmode.LinearOpMode; import com.qualcomm.robotcore.eventloop.opmode.TeleOp; import com.qualcomm.robotcore.hardware.DcMotor; import com.qualcomm.robotcore.hardware.DcMotorEx; import com.qualcomm.robotcore.hardware.Servo; @TeleOp(name = "Actuator Control Guide", group = "Guides") public class ActuatorControlGuide extends LinearOpMode { private DcMotorEx liftMotor; private Servo intakeServo; @Override public void runOpMode() { liftMotor = hardwareMap.get(DcMotorEx.class, "liftMotor"); intakeServo = hardwareMap.get(Servo.class, "intakeServo"); // Establish motor initial configuration liftMotor.setDirection(DcMotor.Direction.FORWARD); liftMotor.setZeroPowerBehavior(DcMotor.ZeroPowerBehavior.BRAKE); liftMotor.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.STOP_AND_RESET_ENCODER); liftMotor.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.RUN_USING_ENCODER); waitForStart(); while (opModeIsActive()) { // Positional target control for vertical lift if (gamepad1.dpad_up) { liftMotor.setTargetPosition(1850); liftMotor.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.RUN_TO_POSITION); liftMotor.setPower(0.9); } else if (gamepad1.dpad_down) { liftMotor.setTargetPosition(10); liftMotor.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.RUN_TO_POSITION); liftMotor.setPower(0.4); } // Dual-position servo deployment if (gamepad1.left_bumper) { intakeServo.setPosition(0.15); // Stowed position } else if (gamepad1.right_bumper) { intakeServo.setPosition(0.85); // Deployed intake position } telemetry.addData("Lift Encoder Position", liftMotor.getCurrentPosition()); telemetry.addData("Lift Velocity (ticks/s)", liftMotor.getVelocity()); telemetry.addData("Servo Target Ratio", intakeServo.getPosition()); telemetry.update(); } } } Motor Oscillates at Target: The internal proportional coefficient k_P in the expansion hub's default RUN_TO_POSITION loop is too aggressive for high-inertia loads. Switch to custom software PIDF controllers or decrease motor maximum allowable power. Encoder Counts Remain Zero Under Rotation: Inspect the 4-pin JST-PH connector seating. If pins 3 and 4 are disconnected or damaged, the hub cannot detect quadrature transitions. Servo Stutters or Drops Controller Connection: Measure battery rail voltage during actuation. Severe voltage sag caused by unbuffered servo stall events will trigger micro-brownouts in the robot controller. Implement current limits or install an auxiliary servo power module.

title: FTC Sensors Guide: Color, Time-of-Flight Distance & Touch Sensors
description: Integration guide for REV Color Sensor v3, 2-meter distance sensors, and limit switches for robust autonomous routines.
body: Robotic perception in FIRST Tech Challenge transforms physical state variables—chassis orientation, game element optical properties, linear slide limits, and obstacle proximity—into digital telemetry. Achieving millisecond-level reaction times and deterministic autonomous routines depends on mastering hardware communication protocols (I²C, Analog, and Digital GPIO) and noise filtering algorithms. FTC robots integrate digital, analog, and bus-oriented sensors across the REV Control Hub and Expansion Hub IO banks: | Sensor Device | Primary Interface | Sensing Principle | Operating Voltage | Subsystem Application | |---|---|---|---:|---| | REV Color Sensor V3 (REV-31-1557) | I²C (Busses 0–3) | Photodiode array (RGB + IR) & proximity LED | 3.3V DC | Sample classification, game piece detection inside intake | | REV 2m Distance Sensor | I²C (Busses 0–3) | Time-of-Flight (ToF) VCSEL laser (VL53L0X) | 3.3V DC | Arena field perimeter alignment, auto parking distance | | REV Magnetic Limit Switch | Digital (Ch 0/1) | Solid-state omnipolar Hall effect | 3.3V DC | Contactless homing for linear lift stages and virtual four-bars | | REV Touch Sensor | Digital (Ch 0/1) | Mechanical SPST snap-action microswitch | 3.3V DC | Hard safety cutoff stops for arms and intake slides | | REV Through-Bore Encoder | Analog / Digital | Absolute magnetic angle & quadrature pulses | 3.3V DC | Coaxial swerve azimuth tracking, dead-wheel odometry pods | | Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) | Internal I²C Bus | 3-axis MEMS gyroscope & accelerometer | 3.3V DC | Closed-loop field-centric heading control and drift compensation | Sensor connections on REV Hubs utilize standardized 4-pin JST-PH connectors. Respecting signal pin assignments prevents permanent damage to board-level transceiver chips: I²C Sensor Bus (4-Pin JST-PH): Pin 1: System Ground (GND) Pin 2: Regulated +3.3V DC Supply (Max 500 mA combined I²C rail) Pin 3: Serial Data Line (SDA) Pin 4: Serial Clock Line (SCL) Digital IO Connector (4-Pin JST-PH): Pin 1: Ground (GND) Pin 2: +3.3V DC Supply (Max 1A combined digital rail) Pin 3: Channel n (Configurable GPIO with internal pull-up) Pin 4: Channel n+1 (Configurable GPIO with internal pull-up) Analog Input Connector (4-Pin JST-PH): Pin 1: Ground (GND) Pin 2: +3.3V DC Supply Pin 3: Analog In 0 ( 0 - 5.0V input range) Pin 4: Analog In 1 ( 0 - 5.0V input range) [Hub I2C Header] Pin 1 (GND) ─────── Sensor Ground Pin 2 (3.3V) ─────── Sensor VCC (+3.3V) Pin 3 (SDA) ─────── Sensor Serial Data Pin 4 (SCL) ─────── Sensor Serial Clock [Hub Digital Header] Pin 1 (GND) ─────── Switch Common (COM) Pin 2 (3.3V) ─────── Auxiliary Indicator LED Pin 3 (DIO) ─────── Normally Open (NO) I²C Hardware Addressing Constraint: Each independent I²C bus on the REV Control Hub and Expansion Hub features its own physical hardware bus controller. If a robot architecture requires two identical sensors sharing a static I²C slave address (for example, two REV Color Sensor V3 units with factory address 0x52 ), they must be plugged into separate hub I²C ports (e.g., Port 0 and Port 1). Attempting to daisy-chain identical addresses onto a single bus creates bus contention and drops telemetry frames. Absolute rotary encoders provide an analog output voltage V_out scaled linearly to shaft angle theta : theta = (frac{V_{out}}{V_{ref}}) * theta_{max} where V_ref = 3.3V and theta_max = 360^circ . Chassis orientation theta_yaw(t) is derived by integrating instantaneous angular yaw velocity omega_z(t) : theta_{yaw}(t) = theta_0 + int_{0}^{t} omega_z(tau) , dtau To eliminate discontinuity errors across the pm 180^circ wrap boundary when feeding error terms into orientation PID controllers: theta_{err} = atan2(sin(theta_{target} - theta_{current}),, cos(theta_{target} - theta_{current})) The following OpMode configures the universal IMU interface, a REV Color Sensor V3 for sample intake detection, and a digital limit switch for elevator homing: package org.firstinspires.ftc.teamcode; import com.qualcomm.hardware.rev.RevColorSensorV3; import com.qualcomm.hardware.rev.RevHubOrientationOnRobot; import com.qualcomm.robotcore.eventloop.opmode.LinearOpMode; import com.qualcomm.robotcore.eventloop.opmode.TeleOp; import com.qualcomm.robotcore.hardware.DigitalChannel; import com.qualcomm.robotcore.hardware.IMU; import org.firstinspires.ftc.robotcore.external.navigation.AngleUnit; import org.firstinspires.ftc.robotcore.external.navigation.DistanceUnit; @TeleOp(name = "Sensors Integration Guide", group = "Guides") public class SensorsIntegrationGuide extends LinearOpMode { private IMU imu; private RevColorSensorV3 intakeSensor; private DigitalChannel liftBottomLimit; @Override public void runOpMode() { // Universal IMU initialization for Control Hub imu = hardwareMap.get(IMU.class, "imu"); IMU.Parameters imuParameters = new IMU.Parameters( new RevHubOrientationOnRobot( RevHubOrientationOnRobot.LogoFacingDirection.UP, RevHubOrientationOnRobot.UsbFacingDirection.FORWARD ) ); imu.initialize(imuParameters); // Optical proximity and color sensor setup intakeSensor = hardwareMap.get(RevColorSensorV3.class, "intakeSensor"); // Digital limit switch configured in input mode liftBottomLimit = hardwareMap.get(DigitalChannel.class, "liftLimit"); liftBottomLimit.setMode(DigitalChannel.Mode.INPUT); waitForStart(); imu.resetYaw(); while (opModeIsActive()) { // Read continuous heading in degrees double robotYaw = imu.getRobotYawPitchRollAngles().getYaw(AngleUnit.DEGREES); // Optical proximity distance in millimeters double proximityMm = intakeSensor.getDistance(DistanceUnit.MM); // Active-low magnetic or touch switch evaluation boolean isLiftAtBase = !liftBottomLimit.getState(); // Evaluate sample possession boolean sampleLoaded = proximityMm < 25.0; telemetry.addData("Heading (Degrees)", "%.2f", robotYaw); telemetry.addData("Proximity Distance (mm)", "%.1f", proximityMm); telemetry.addData("Sample Secured", sampleLoaded); telemetry.addData("Lift Baseline Triggered", isLiftAtBase); telemetry.update(); } } } I²C Bus Timeout Crash ( I2cController.readStatus: transaction error ): Long, unshielded sensor cables picking up inductive noise from motor power lines can cause the hub hardware bus controller to hang. Ensure sensor wires do not bundle directly against 12V motor leads, and twist SDA/SCL wire pairs with GND. Color Sensor Flickering Readings: Ambient stage lighting in competition arenas fluctuates significantly compared to build space fluorescent fixtures. Normalize optical readings by calculating chromatic ratios: Red Ratio = (R / R + G + B), quad Blue Ratio = (B / R + G + B) IMU Yaw Drifts Over Match Duration: Excessive chassis vibration can saturate MEMS gyroscopes. Mount the Control Hub onto 30A–40A durometer silicone vibration isolation standoffs to dampen high-frequency mechanical shock.

title: Mecanum Drivetrains: Geometry and Holonomic Motion Principles
description: 45-degree roller mechanics, robot center-of-gravity placement, rotation kinematics and vibration damping over field obstacles.
body: The drivetrain chassis serves as the physical and mechanical foundation of an FTC robot, determining translational agility, pushing force, and trajectory precision during both 30-second autonomous and 2-minute teleoperated periods. Selecting the optimal drive architecture—Mecanum, Tank, or Coaxial Swerve—and mastering inverse kinematics and dead-wheel odometry algorithms is essential for elite match play. Drivetrain configurations present distinct engineering trade-offs regarding mechanical complexity, friction characteristics, and software control overhead: | Drivetrain Type | Holonomic Mobility | Drive Actuator Count | Traction & Pushing Force | Mechanical Complexity | Software & Tuning Difficulty | Primary Match Application | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | Mecanum Drive | Yes (Omnidirectional translation & rotation) | 4 independent planetary motors | Moderate (Susceptible to lateral defensive pushing) | Low (Direct axle mounting to gearboxes) | Moderate (Standard Mecanum kinematic model) | Standard FTC baseline; excels at agile cycling and scoring alignment | | Tank / Skid-Steer | No (Non-holonomic; forward, reverse, tank turn) | 2, 4, or 6 gearmotors | Very High (High-durometer roughtop or rubber tread) | Minimal (Spur gears or timing belt pulleys) | Low (Direct differential drive control) | Defense-heavy matches, obstacle traversal, heavy chassis designs | | Coaxial Swerve | Yes (Independent steering angle & drive velocity per pod) | 4 drive + 4 steer (Brushless or Smart Servos) | High (Treaded wheels with active steering vectoring) | Extreme (Bevel gear differentials, slip rings/continuous wiring) | High (Individual pod azimuth PID + vector field odometry) | Cutting-edge high-resource teams seeking uncompromised traction and maneuverability | | 3 / 4-Wheel Omni | Yes (90° perpendicular passive rollers) | 3 or 4 motors | Low (Low lateral resistance) | Low | Moderate | Ultra-lightweight chassis requiring rapid circular agility | Crucial Mecanum Roller Geometry: Mecanum wheels must be installed in an "X-Pattern" configuration when viewed from top-down . The contact rollers touching the mat floor must angle inward toward the geometric center of the robot. If accidentally mounted in an "O-Pattern", the lateral force vectors cancel destructively, eliminating strafing capability. To command a robot with longitudinal velocity v_x , lateral velocity v_y , and angular yaw rate omega_z (rad/s) in the robot coordinate frame, target wheel surface linear velocities are computed through the classic kinematic matrix: v_{FL} = v_x - v_y - omega_z (L_x + L_y) v_{FR} = v_x + v_y + omega_z (L_x + L_y) v_{BL} = v_x + v_y - omega_z (L_x + L_y) v_{BR} = v_x - v_y + omega_z (L_x + L_y) Where: L_x : Longitudinal half-track distance from chassis centroid to wheel axle centers (m). L_y : Lateral half-track distance from chassis centroid to wheel contact centerlines (m). v_FL, v_FR, v_BL, v_BR : Commanded linear velocity targets for Front-Left, Front-Right, Back-Left, and Back-Right wheels. During compound maneuvers (strafing while rotating under full forward throttle), individual wheel commands can exceed the hardware ceiling [-1.0, 1.0] . Normalizing against the maximum component preserves heading vectors and avoids unpredictable trajectory distortion: v_{max} = max(|v_{FL}|, |v_{FR}|, |v_{BL}|, |v_{BR}|, 1.0) v_i' = (v_i / v_{max)} quad forall i in {FL, FR, BL, BR} Field-centric drive control decouples joystick directions from chassis rotation, allowing operators to drive relative to the field perimeter regardless of where the robot intake points. Raw gamepad joystick inputs ( J_x, J_y ) are rotated into the robot coordinate frame using current IMU yaw angle theta : v_x = J_x cos(-theta) - J_y sin(-theta) v_y = J_x sin(-theta) + J_y cos(-theta) Because Mecanum passive rollers experience intermittent slippage during aggressive accelerations, drive motor encoders cannot provide deterministic pose tracking for autonomous routines. FTC teams implement 3-wheel unpowered dead-wheel odometry pods pressed into the soft foam tiles via sprung suspensions. ┌─────────── Front Chassis Frame ───────────┐ │ │ Left Dead Wheel (L) Right Dead Wheel (R) │ │ │ Perpendicular Dead Wheel (C) │ └───────────────────────────────────────────┘ Pose updates across discrete sample intervals Delta t follow arc-length approximations: Delta theta = (Delta L - Delta R / B) Delta y_{local} = (Delta L + Delta R / 2) Delta x_{local} = Delta C - D_{perp} * Delta theta Where: B : Track width between left and right tracking wheels (calibrated in mm). D_perp : Perpendicular displacement from robot center of rotation to the transverse tracking wheel. Delta L, Delta R, Delta C : Incremental linear arc displacements reported by high-resolution encoders (such as REV Through-Bore Encoders). package org.firstinspires.ftc.teamcode; import com.qualcomm.hardware.rev.RevHubOrientationOnRobot; import com.qualcomm.robotcore.eventloop.opmode.LinearOpMode; import com.qualcomm.robotcore.eventloop.opmode.TeleOp; import com.qualcomm.robotcore.hardware.DcMotor; import com.qualcomm.robotcore.hardware.DcMotorEx; import com.qualcomm.robotcore.hardware.IMU; import org.firstinspires.ftc.robotcore.external.navigation.AngleUnit; @TeleOp(name = "Field-Centric Mecanum Controller", group = "Guides") public class FieldCentricMecanumController extends LinearOpMode { @Override public void runOpMode() { DcMotorEx motorFL = hardwareMap.get(DcMotorEx.class, "motorFL"); DcMotorEx motorFR = hardwareMap.get(DcMotorEx.class, "motorFR"); DcMotorEx motorBL = hardwareMap.get(DcMotorEx.class, "motorBL"); DcMotorEx motorBR = hardwareMap.get(DcMotorEx.class, "motorBR"); // Reverse left motors to align positive power with forward chassis motion motorFL.setDirection(DcMotor.Direction.REVERSE); motorBL.setDirection(DcMotor.Direction.REVERSE); motorFR.setDirection(DcMotor.Direction.FORWARD); motorBR.setDirection(DcMotor.Direction.FORWARD); // Active electromagnetic braking for immediate stopping motorFL.setZeroPowerBehavior(DcMotor.ZeroPowerBehavior.BRAKE); motorFR.setZeroPowerBehavior(DcMotor.ZeroPowerBehavior.BRAKE); motorBL.setZeroPowerBehavior(DcMotor.ZeroPowerBehavior.BRAKE); motorBR.setZeroPowerBehavior(DcMotor.ZeroPowerBehavior.BRAKE); IMU imu = hardwareMap.get(IMU.class, "imu"); IMU.Parameters imuConfig = new IMU.Parameters(new RevHubOrientationOnRobot( RevHubOrientationOnRobot.LogoFacingDirection.UP, RevHubOrientationOnRobot.UsbFacingDirection.FORWARD)); imu.initialize(imuConfig); waitForStart(); while (opModeIsActive()) { double y = -gamepad1.left_stick_y; // Invert joystick Y convention double x = gamepad1.left_stick_x * 1.1; // Counteract lateral roller drag double rx = gamepad1.right_stick_x; if (gamepad1.guide || gamepad1.options) { imu.resetYaw(); } double headingRadians = imu.getRobotYawPitchRollAngles().getYaw(AngleUnit.RADIANS); // Vector rotation into robot-centric frame double rotX = x * Math.cos(-headingRadians) - y * Math.sin(-headingRadians); double rotY = x * Math.sin(-headingRadians) + y * Math.cos(-headingRadians); // Mecanum inverse kinematics calculation double maxComponent = Math.max(Math.abs(rotY) + Math.abs(rotX) + Math.abs(rx), 1.0); double flPower = (rotY + rotX + rx) / maxComponent; double blPower = (rotY - rotX + rx) / maxComponent; double frPower = (rotY - rotX - rx) / maxComponent; double brPower = (rotY + rotX - rx) / maxComponent; motorFL.setPower(flPower); motorBL.setPower(blPower); motorFR.setPower(frPower); motorBR.setPower(brPower); telemetry.addData("Heading Angle (Deg)", Math.toDegrees(headingRadians)); telemetry.addData("FL / FR Power", "%.2f / %.2f", flPower, frPower); telemetry.addData("BL / BR Power", "%.2f / %.2f", blPower, brPower); telemetry.update(); } } } Unwanted Turning Drift While Driving Straight: Calculate the physical Center of Mass (CoM). If the battery pack or heavy lift arm biases weight heavily toward one side, the high-normal-force wheels exhibit greater tractive resistance, causing yaw deflection. Counterbalance the chassis or implement closed-loop gyro heading lock in software. Odometry Tracking Wheel Bounce: Foam tiles compress under robot weight. Ensure tracking pods use constant-force springs calibrated between 2.0 N and 3.0 N. Excessive spring force lifts the chassis off the floor, whereas insufficient preload causes the wheel to lose contact during rapid direction reversals. Drivetrain Sluggishness Under Low Battery: Monitor internal battery sensor logs. If battery voltage drops under 10.5V, high current draw during 4-motor acceleration pushes the hub toward brownout cutoffs. Replace battery packs every 2–3 match cycles.

title: Dead Wheel Odometry Pods: Absolute Robot Field Localization
description: Spring-loaded unpowered tracking wheel pods, optical encoders, and eliminating wheel slip drift in FTC.
body: Odometry uses measurement wheels (dead wheels) and encoders to estimate robot position instead of trusting drivetrain motion alone. Because a dead wheel does not propel the robot, it usually slips less during acceleration and rotation. A common three-wheel layout has two parallel wheels measuring forward/back motion and one perpendicular wheel measuring lateral motion. An IMU supplies heading; software combines heading and encoder displacement to update pose (x, y, θ) . Mount each pod to a rigid portion of the frame, away from possible field collisions. The wheel needs spring-loaded contact with enough force to stay planted: too little force causes skipped counts, while too much force adds drag and can bend the bracket. Measure actual wheel circumference after the tire is installed. Ticks per inch equals encoder counts per wheel revolution divided by circumference. Derive counts per wheel revolution from the encoder specification, quadrature decoding factor, and encoder revolutions per wheel revolution; avoid applying a gearbox or quadrature factor twice if the reported count already includes it. | Layout | Strength | Risk | Good fit | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Two parallel wheels + IMU | Measures forward motion and heading | Cannot directly measure strafe | Differential drive | | Two parallel + one perpendicular | Direct strafe measurement | Requires accurate offsets | Mecanum or swerve FTC robots | | Two wheels + drive encoders | Saves frame space | Drive-wheel slip remains | Tight frames at moderate speed | Measure real travel by pushing the robot 48 inches along each axis several times, averaging the results, and tuning ticksPerInch . Place the robot on a marked square, rotate exactly 10 turns, and compare IMU angle with physical angle to derive the heading scale. Measure each pod's distance from the robot's rotation center; an offset error produces a turn-position error even when encoder counts are correct. In code, read all encoder snapshots from one loop cycle, convert ticks to inches, then integrate local deltas using the cycle's mean heading. Normalize angles to [-π, π) so 359° to 0° does not create a false large turn. Log ticks, velocity, heading, and pose at 10–20 samples per second. Counts while stationary indicate vibration, a loose encoder cable, or an overly sensitive input path. A forward run that accumulates lateral error points to a skewed perpendicular pod or a pod that is not parallel to its intended axis. Re-tighten hardware, inspect tire wear, and leave a strain-relief loop in every encoder cable. Odometry is an estimate: reset pose at a known autonomous starting mark and use AprilTags or field lines for correction when the match strategy requires it.

title: Linear Slide Cascades: Multi-Stage Extension and Rigging
description: Continuous vs Cascade rigging trade-offs, UHMWPE/Kevlar cord routing, and deflection prevention on stage extensions.
body: A linear slide converts motor rotation into translation for a scoring lift or an arm that reaches into a workspace. A typical assembly has a fixed rail, moving stages, pulleys, a cable, and a winding drum. Select rails for travel, fully extended stiffness, and off-axis loading—not only for a static load rating. Both sides must remain parallel; a twisted rail can bind even when the motor has enough torque. | Style | Motion model | Advantage | Trade-off | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Cascade | Stages move nearly together | Fast and compact | Complex cable paths | | Continuous | One stage leads and pulls the next | Easy to understand and service | Different stage speed/load distribution | | Single stage | Drum pulls one carriage directly | Few parts, simple tuning | Limited travel | For a cascade, anchor the cable to the frame and route it over pulleys on each stage according to the slide manufacturer's diagram. Changing an anchor point changes direction and travel ratio. For a continuous rig, verify each stage's order before attaching the motor. Either style needs a positive recovery method or counteracting cable so descent remains controlled; do not depend entirely on gravity when the mechanism can tilt. Start with static lift force F = m × g , then add friction and a suitable safety factor. Approximate minimum drum torque as τ = F × r / η , where r is effective winding radius and η is transmission efficiency. If cable layers overlap, r grows while winding: speed rises but pulling force falls, changing motor load during a stroke. A drum wide enough for one cable layer gives more predictable behavior. Use gearing to balance speed and torque, and check the motor over its real duty cycle rather than only its stall torque. Mount rails parallel and hand-slide the carriage through its complete travel before adding cable. Deburr pulley edges, keep cable away from sharp aluminum, secure each end with a suitable clamp or knot, and mark the cable to detect creep. Equalize both sides, then lift a light load at low power; measure skew and correct it before high-speed testing. Add mechanical stops and a home sensor. Set software soft limits from encoder position, but never treat a soft limit as a mechanical stop replacement. Inspect frayed cable, loose pulley fasteners, and play after every practice session. Keep hands out of pinch zones, disconnect power before service, and lower loads safely before removing cable. If one side moves slower, stop immediately: continuing to power the slide can twist rails or snap the cable.

title: FTC Intake and Transfer Mechanisms: Roller Geometries and Compliant Wheels
description: Compliant wheel durometer selection, silicone surgical tubing rollers, contact angles, and anti-jam sensor logic.
body: An intake brings a game element from the field into the robot; a transfer moves it from that intake to storage or a scoring mechanism. Both parts should form one continuous transport path: roller speed, clearance, and guides determine whether an element is captured or ejected. Game rules change each season, so measure the real element's size, mass, and compliance before finalizing geometry. | Mechanism | Best fit | Strength | Limitation | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Rubber roller | Rigid element with clear contact | Fast capture, compact layout | Can eject element when too fast | | Compliant wheel | Misaligned or deformable element | Tolerates error, more contact | Wear and pinch force change | | Conveyor | Long transfer distance | Consistent direction | Needs tension and alignment | | Passive funnel | Gathering into a narrow mouth | No extra motor | Can jam at a steep angle | Roller surface speed is v = π × diameter × rpm / 60 . Start near the robot's approach speed and test both slower and faster settings instead of selecting the highest RPM. Clearance should create friction without deforming the element or stalling the motor. Support long rollers at both ends to limit shaft deflection, and shield drive parts from wiring and operators' hands. Use a flared guide at the entrance, narrowing gradually toward the working width. Avoid sharp corners, tall steps, and dead gaps between rollers. When two stages run together, make the downstream stage receive the element quickly without pulling so hard that it rotates. Add an access opening so a jammed element can be removed without dismantling the robot. An optical sensor or limit switch can report arrival; test reflective and dark elements before trusting its signal. Test at least three approach directions, several off-center positions, and multiple drive speeds. Record successful captures divided by total attempts. On a jam, stop or briefly reverse the roller through driver control, and use a time limit to prevent motor overheating. Check current and temperature after a test series, then inspect compliant wheels for wear or debris. Disconnect robot power before placing a hand in the element path; software must not be the only safety measure.

title: Smart Servo Comparison: REV SRS vs Axon Mini & Axon Max
description: Torque specs, titanium geartrains, 6V vs 12V power rails, programmable limits, and BEC current protection.
body: REV Smart Robot Servo and many Axon servos use familiar PWM control while integrating their own position sensing and control electronics. That internal feedback lets a positional servo regulate its output shaft, but it does not mean the FTC controller can read the actual angle. Capabilities vary by exact model and configuration: confirm supported modes, voltage, range, and programming method in its documentation. Internal feedback does not create unlimited torque or remove the need for sound mechanical alignment. | Property | PWM servo | Smart servo | Design meaning | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Command | Pulse width | Pulse width on REV SRS and many Axon models | Confirm the exact control mode | | Feedback | Usually not exposed | Internal position feedback; external reporting varies | Do not assume readable angle | | Configuration | Model-dependent | Programmable modes and limits on supported models | Record each servo's setup | | Power wiring | Signal, V+ and GND | Connector and current needs vary by model | Check polarity and supply rating | Read the datasheet for the exact model before wiring. Axon and REV products can differ in connector, voltage, angle range, speed, and programming procedure; “smart” does not guarantee compatible settings. Use a servo supply with enough current and wiring rated for the load. A startup voltage drop can cause erratic behavior or reset control electronics. Follow current FTC rules and the hub manufacturer's instructions when choosing power distribution. Install the horn at the mechanism's neutral mechanical position before commanding an angle. Set software limits inside the hard-stop range so gears are not forced against a stop. Low speed and acceleration near an endpoint reduce impact; for high-inertia loads, use a motion profile or state-based control instead of an abrupt angle step. Log commanded positions and any feedback actually exposed by the hardware. If motion stops, check supply, connections, configuration, and mechanical binding before replacing the servo. Evaluate torque at the horn, not only a vendor's advertised stall number. Test holding at several angles, measure temperature after repeated cycles, and watch for backlash. A mechanical latch should locate or retain a mechanism, not force the servo to hold a heavy load continuously. Secure cables against twisting, protect connectors from impacts, and record firmware versions in the robot build log. Disconnect power before removing a horn or clearing a jam.

title: 12V Power Distribution & Battery Harnessing: FTC Electrical Safety Standards
description: Main power switch rules, 20A fuse inspection, AWG14 high-strand silicon wires, XT30/Anderson, and brownout mitigation.
body: Electrical power distribution is the mission-critical foundation of any competitive FIRST Tech Challenge (FTC) robot. A well-engineered electrical harness must reliably deliver transient peak currents between 20A and 40A to four drivetrain gearmotors and heavy manipulator mechanisms without inducing brownout resets, while satisfying rigorous Robot Inspection safety requirements. FTC rules mandate using exactly one approved 12V nominal NiMH battery pack (or approved equivalent chemistry). Electrical current flows from the battery pack through an integrated 20A inline fuse and an accessible main power switch before energizing the REV Control Hub, which cascades 12V DC power to a secondary REV Expansion Hub via XT30 connectors. 12V NiMH Battery ── 20A Inline Fuse ── Main Switch ── REV Control Hub (XT30 In) ├─ Drivetrain DC Motors (x4) ├─ 5V Servo Ports / Smart Servos ├─ Digital / I2C / Analog Sensors └─ REV Expansion Hub (XT30 Out ── XT30 In) | Component | Engineering Recommendation | Safety & Compliance Function | | --- | --- | --- | | Main Power Wires | High-strand silicone copper wire (AWG 14) | Handles thermal spikes, offers tight bend radius, minimizes resistance | | Battery Connectors | Anderson Powerpole (15A/45A) or XT30 | Must be ratcheting-crimped with retention clips installed | | Circuit Protection | 20A automotive blade or cartridge fuse | Inspect fuse housing integrity and continuity before official inspection | | Main Power Switch | REV Main Switch or approved rotary switch | Rigidly mounted, immediately accessible to field referees, marked ON/OFF | During aggressive maneuvers, rapid direction reversals, or mechanism stalls, motor current draw surges violently. If the supply voltage at the Control Hub input terminals drops below 7.5V–8.0V: The internal Android Single Board Computer (SBC) triggers an emergency shutdown or reboot cycle. Wi-Fi Direct or REV 9-Axis communication disconnects from the Driver Station, leaving the robot stranded dead on the field for 30–60 seconds. Key mitigation practices: Minimize Total Loop Resistance : Eliminate twist-and-tape joints or low-grade push terminals. Every connection must use certified crimp connectors or dual heat-shrunk solder joints. Shorten Wiring Lengths : Keep the high-current wire run between battery terminals, the main power switch, and the primary Hub under 25–30 cm. Dedicated Daisy-Chain Run : Power the secondary Expansion Hub through a direct AWG 16 silicone XT30 cable instead of splicing auxiliary loads into the main battery leads. Software Slew-Rate Limiting : Apply software acceleration ramping on drivetrain DC motors to prevent simultaneous stall-current draws during sudden stick inputs. Verify open-circuit battery voltage with a digital multimeter (DMM): only load batteries measuring between 13.2V and 13.8V onto the robot. Confirm positive mechanical locking on all XT30 connectors and verify Anderson Powerpole retention clips are fully engaged. Perform a physical tug-and-wiggle check along the primary power harness while the robot is energized to detect intermittent wire fractures or loose spade lugs. Fasten the battery enclosure with dual high-tensile velcro straps to ensure zero battery displacement during aggressive field collisions.

title: End-Effector Design: Claws, Passive Latching, and Active Rollers
description: Active pinch claws, passive latch geometry, high-friction PU foam pads, and servo positioning precision.
body: In FIRST Tech Challenge (FTC), the end-effector is the critical interface between the robot and season game elements (cones, blocks, pixels, or samples). Designing an effective end-effector requires balancing rapid acquisition time, retention force against aggressive robot acceleration, mechanical weight constraints, and passive compliance that accommodates alignment errors. Depending on the geometry, rigidity, and surface friction of the target game elements, competitive teams deploy three primary mechanical architectures: ┌── Active Pinch Claw ──────── 4-Bar Parallel Linkage + Smart PWM Servo │ End-Effector ──┼── Active Roller Intake ───── Compliant TPU Wheels + High-RPM Motor Drive │ └── Passive Latch Mechanism ── Chamfered Ramp Geometry + Return Springs | Mechanism Type | Cycle Acquisition Time | Weight & Complexity | Primary Strengths | Technical Trade-offs | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Pinch Claw (Active) | 0.2s – 0.5s | Moderate (150–300g) | High grip retention, precise orientation control | Demands accurate drivetrain alignment | | Active Rollers (Flywheel) | < 0.1s | High (300–600g) | Wide intake acceptance window, seamless pull-in | High power consumption, bulky envelope | | Passive Latch (Geometry) | Instantaneous | Very Low (< 100g) | Zero motor/servo ports consumed, featherweight | Requires dedicated ejector rod or reverse motion | The static coefficient of friction ( \mu ) between the gripper pads and the game piece dictates the clamping torque required from your actuators: Polyurethane (PU) Foam & Silicone Sheet : Delivers high friction coefficients ( \mu > 1.2 ) against slick molded plastic game elements. The compressive elasticity of PU foam distributes load over curved surfaces, preventing slippage under high linear acceleration. 3D Printed TPU (Shore 95A / 85A) : Ideal for custom contoured fingers. Infill geometries (such as gyroid or hexagonal lattices) provide engineered compliance, allowing gripper fingers to passively deflect and wrap securely around irregular objects without permanent deformation. Silicone Surgical Tubing on Spindles : A proven, field-repairable solution for active roller shafts, maintaining consistent traction even as field dust accumulates throughout qualification matches. Smart Servo Endpoint Tuning : Utilizing programmable servos (such as REV Smart Robot Servos or Axon Mini/Max) allows software developers to configure software travel limits (Stow, Wide-Open, Pre-Clamp, Secure-Clamp). Properly tuned endpoints eliminate motor stalling, preventing thermal shutdown and battery voltage drops. Optical Break-Beam & Distance Sensors : Embedding a miniature time-of-flight (ToF) or infrared distance sensor inside the gripper cradle enables automated clamping. Once the object breaches the threshold distance (10–20mm), the Robot Controller initiates an instant clamping command in under 20ms, bypassing driver reaction latency entirely. Mechanical Undercut & Anti-Drop Geometry : Designing physical gripper teeth with a slight reverse taper (3°–5° undercut) ensures that rapid chassis deceleration forces the game element deeper into the gripping socket rather than dislodging it.

title: FTC Match Structure & Alliance Scoring Strategy
description: Deep dive into 30s Autonomous, 2-minute Driver-Controlled period, and 30s Endgame scoring optimization.
body: An official FIRST Tech Challenge (FTC) match spans exactly 2 minutes and 30 seconds of high-intensity competition between two opposing alliances (Red Alliance vs. Blue Alliance), with each alliance composed of two distinct team robots. Maximizing alliance score demands far more than raw mechanism velocity; it requires a deep technical grasp of match flow phases, disciplined cycle time budgeting, symbiotic alliance communication, and ruthless penalty avoidance. FTC matches are orchestrated automatically by the tournament Field Control System (FCS), following a strict chronological progression: [ 0:00 - 0:30 ] ────────► [ 0:30 - 0:38 ] ────────► [ 0:38 - 2:08 ] ────────► [ 2:08 - 2:38 ] Autonomous Period Field Transition TeleOp Period Endgame Period (Pre-programmed - 30s) (Referee Pause ~8s) (Driver-Controlled - 90s) (High-Value Bonus - 30s) | Match Phase | Duration | Operational Constraints | Strategic Core Objective | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Autonomous | 30 Seconds | Pre-programmed sensor feedback, computer vision & odometry | Secure baseline autonomous bonus, score preload elements, park accurately | | Field Transition | ~8 Seconds | Hands off gamepads; field referees audit positions | Maintain stable arm posture, select TeleOp OpMode on Driver Station | | TeleOp (Driver) | 90 Seconds | Dual gamepads input active; manual robot piloting | Execute rapid scoring cycles, supply alliance partners, control field traffic | | Endgame | Final 30 Seconds | Sub-phase of TeleOp; specialized tasks unlocked | High-elevation hanging/pull-up, drone launch, specialized parking bonuses | In competitive TeleOp, overall alliance scoring is governed by total completed cycles. Every cycle consists of four distinct operational legs: Acquisition -> Field Transit -> Alignment & Scoring -> Return Transit : Zonal Partitioning : Both alliance teams must delineate clear operating boundaries prior to match queuing. One robot should dominate close-proximity rapid cycling, while the alliance partner executes long-range element feeding or dedicated placement. Traffic Bottleneck Mitigation : Driving paths through field arches, trusses, or perimeter choke points must follow agreed-upon flow rules (e.g., clockwise transit loops) to eliminate head-on gridlock between alliance partners. Endgame Cutoff Discipline : The Drive Coach must enforce a strict point of no return. Never initiate a fresh intake cycle with under 12–15 seconds on the match timer. Transitioning immediately to the climb structure ensures secure latching before the terminal buzzer sounds. A single Major Penalty (30 penalty points gifted to the opposing alliance) can erase the point advantage built during an entire Autonomous phase: Strict Possession Limits : Enforce strict hardware or software limit interlocks. Never herd, push, or contain more game elements than allowed by season rules (typically 1 or 2 items). Optical sensors inside the intake should actively disable rollers when full capacity is reached. Opponent Protected Zones : Avoid contact with opponent robots when they are stationed inside designated protected field boundaries (such as scoring backdrops or submersible zones). Post-Buzzer Inaction : All motor and servo pulse trains must cease instantly upon the conclusion of match sound effects. Continued mechanism operation incurs severe penalty assessments or disqualification of Endgame scoring tasks.

title: Building a Winning 15-Page FTC Engineering Portfolio
description: Structuring the engineering design process, iterative failures, budget management and outreach documentation in 15 pages.
body: In the FIRST Tech Challenge (FTC) judging system, the Engineering Portfolio is the single most decisive document for prestigious judged awards such as the Inspire Award, Think Award, Innovate Award, and Design Award. Because judges have mere minutes during their initial deliberation rounds to digest your season's work, structuring your 15 pages with dense quantitative evidence, clear visual hierarchies, and rigorous adherence to FIRST guidelines is paramount. FIRST enforces an uncompromising constraint: judges are instructed to discard or ignore any pages beyond the 15-page limit. To capture maximum scoring across multiple award rubrics, allocate your page budget deliberately: [Page 1] Team Identity, Member Roles & Season Engineering Goals [Pages 2-8] Engineering Design Process (EDP) per Subsystem (Drivetrain, Intake, Slides, Claw) [Pages 9-11] Software Architecture, Autonomous Odometry & Motion Control (Control Award) [Pages 12-13] Community Outreach, Mentorship & STEM Industry Connections (Connect / Motivate) [Pages 14-15] Team Sustainability, Budget Management & Strategic Growth (Business Plan) | Portfolio Section | Recommended Budget | Target Judging Rubric | Essential Evidence Required | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Team Identity & Summary | 1 Page | Culture & Gracious Professionalism | Member roster, individual responsibilities, overarching season goals | | Mechanical EDP Iterations | 6 – 7 Pages | Think, Innovate, Design Awards | CAD cross-sections, trade studies, load-testing graphs, failure logs | | Software & Control Systems | 2 – 3 Pages | Control Award | State machine flowcharts, PIDF tuning step responses, vision pipelines | | Outreach & Professional Connect | 2 Pages | Connect & Motivate Awards | Quantitative community reach, engineering mentor logs, student impact | | Business Plan & Sustainability | 2 Pages | Strategic Longevity | Bill of materials (BOM), cash-flow balance sheet, sponsor pipeline | Judges do not reward robots that appear magically flawless on day one; they reward documented proof of learning through iterative failure : The Four-Stage Subsystem Narrative : For every primary robot mechanism, document four distinct evolutionary stages: Problem Formulation : Specific mechanical requirements (e.g., target reach height, payload mass, cycle time threshold). Preliminary Prototyping (V1) : Initial laser-cut plywood or 3D-printed proofs of concept. Root-Cause Failure Analysis : Honest dissection of design shortcomings (e.g., cable binding under off-axis load, gear stripping). Engineered Refinement (V2/V3) : Final machined aluminum geometry, bearing support additions, and measured empirical benchmark improvements. Quantify Everything : Replace subjective statements like "Our intake improved significantly" with verified engineering metrics: "Intake acquisition latency decreased from 2.4s (V1 standard servo) to 0.42s (V3 compliant Shore 95A TPU wheels paired with a laser ToF distance trigger)" . Information Density via Visual Callouts : Replace dense text walls with exploded CAD renderings featuring numbered callout boxes pointing directly to key engineering innovations. Typographic Discipline : Maintain a minimum legible font size of 10pt with clean sans-serif typography, structured grid alignments, and high-contrast color palettes suitable for dim judging rooms. Mandatory Header Verification : Ensure your 4-digit or 5-digit FTC Team Number and Team Name appear prominently in the header or footer of every single page.

title: Mastering the FTC Judging Interview Presentation
description: Crafting a memorable 5-minute presentation, role delegation among members, and handling technical Q&A gracefully.
body: The judging interview in the FIRST Tech Challenge represents the primary opportunity for teams to articulate their engineering design process, software innovations, collaborative teamwork, and STEM community outreach. Awards like the Inspire Award, Think Award, Innovate Award, Design Award, Control Award, Connect Award, and Motivate Award rely heavily on the interview alongside the team's Engineering Portfolio. A typical judging session runs for 10 to 15 minutes in a private room with a panel of volunteer judges. The standard agenda consists of: 5-Minute Uninterrupted Presentation: The team delivers their rehearsed pitch covering all facets of their season. 5 to 10 Minutes Technical Q&A: Judges ask detailed technical and process questions regarding robot design, failure modes, coding architectures, and outreach metrics. Novice teams often spend excessive time detailing team history or focusing exclusively on a single sub-mechanism. A structured breakdown ensures balanced coverage across mechanical engineering, software control, and outreach initiatives: | Segment | Duration | Primary Focus | Visual Artifact | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | 1. Hook & Introduction | 30 seconds | Team identity, season thesis, headline robot metric | Team logo banner, robot branding | | 2. Mechanical Design & CAD | 90 seconds | Chassis layout, intake/outtake mechanics, iteration cycle | Exploded CAD renders, broken prototype iterations | | 3. Autonomous & Control Systems | 75 seconds | Odometry localization, motion profiling, computer vision | Telemetry plots, vision target overlay captures | | 4. Outreach & Sustainability | 60 seconds | Community workshops, team budget, sponsorship model | Engineering Portfolio outreach page, sponsor map | | 5. Conclusion & Q&A Handoff | 45 seconds | Next milestones, gratitude, direct transition to Q&A | Open table of contents in Portfolio, eye contact | Judges evaluate whether students independently developed solutions or relied passively on mentors. Teams should format responses using an engineering-driven three-tier framework: Problem and Constraints: Clarify the physical or computational bottleneck encountered (e.g., intake slippage during rapid directional transitions). Quantitative Trade-off: Explain why specific design alternatives were rejected in favor of the current iteration based on data (e.g., motor stall torque, durometer ratings, amp draw). Validation and Iteration: Present the measurable result recorded in the Engineering Portfolio after deploying the modification. [Problem Identified] ──> [Empirical Testing Data] ──> [Selected Solution via Trade-off] │ ▼ [Portfolio Page Reference] Central Robot Placement: Keep the robot accessible on the center table. Ensure power is safely disengaged while mechanisms remain free to articulate by hand during explanations. Physical Prototypes on Hand: Bring failed 3D printed brackets, stripped gears, or bent carbon fiber links. Passing physical iterations to judges demonstrates continuous improvement. Shared Speaking Roles: Do not let a single spokesperson dominate. Ensure mechanical, programming, driving, and business leads speak directly to their respective specialties. Handling Unknowns: When asked a question outside the scope of current testing, reply honestly: "We have not benchmarked that configuration yet due to time constraints, but our working hypothesis is... and it is queued for our post-qualifier sprint."

title: FTC Quantitative Match Scouting & Alliance Selection Strategy
description: Quantitative OPR tracking, autonomous consistency scoring, pit scouting interviews, and building data-driven pick lists.
body: Scouting in the FIRST Tech Challenge is not merely casual observation from the stands; it is the structured collection, normalization, and statistical analysis of field data. A robust scouting operation serves two tactical objectives: Qualification Match Pre-planning: Identifying synergy, cycle paths, and spatial bottlenecks between two alliance partners before stepping onto the playing field. Playoff Alliance Selection Picklist Architecture: Constructing an empirical picklist based on verified scoring rates, eliminating recency bias and subjective guesswork. A standardized scouting sheet separates gameplay into distinct game periods and isolates key mechanical and operational attributes: | Category | Primary Metric | Calculation / Tracking Method | Strategic Significance | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Autonomous | Pre-load & Spike Success Rate | (Successful Scored Pre-loads / Total Match Attempts) * 100% | Validates computer vision reliability and dead-reckoning odometry accuracy | | Autonomous | Parking / Navigation Consistency | Discrete point value achieved per match | Confirms ability to avoid colliding with alliance partners during transit | | TeleOp | Scoring Cycle Time | Total TeleOp Active Driving Time (seconds) / Valid Elements Scored | Reflects intake reliability, driver dexterity, and outtake velocity | | TeleOp | Element Drop & Miss Frequency | Dropped Elements / (Acquired Elements + Dropped Elements) | Highlights grip stability under violent lateral acceleration | | Endgame | Rigging Hang / Suspension Speed | Suspension level achieved and seconds elapsed to lock mechanism | Establishes critical point deltas in the final 30 seconds of the match | | Discipline | Penalty Propensity | Minor and Major penalty points conceded per match | Filters out high-scoring teams whose foul points negate net alliance margin | To isolate individual team contributions within a two-team alliance, teams construct a system of linear equations modeling Offensive Power Rating (OPR): [Match 1]: Team_A + Team_B = Alliance_1_Score [Match 2]: Team_A + Team_C = Alliance_2_Score ... [Match N]: Team_X + Team_Y = Alliance_N_Score Because total OPR can be skewed by opponent penalty points or partner disconnects, advanced scouts compute Component OPR (cOPR) by breaking match totals into separate vectors for Autonomous scoring, TeleOp cycle output, and Endgame suspension points. Operational consistency is evaluated using the standard deviation ( \sigma ) of TeleOp cycle counts: \sigma < 1.5 : High reliability, predictable cycle output, low mechanical failure risk. \sigma > 4.0 : High variance, frequently prone to jammed intakes, loose belt tension, or software disconnects. Fifteen minutes prior to match queuing, the Drive Coach must meet with the alliance partner to establish concrete operational boundaries: Autonomous Trajectory De-confliction: Map tile-by-tile coordinate vectors for both robots during the 30-second autonomous window. If paths overlap in the central depot or scoring backdrop, the team with the lower autonomous cOPR executes a secondary failsafe script (safe park only). TeleOp Traffic Lane Allocation: Designate one robot to the exterior perimeter corridor and the other to the interior lane. Right-of-Way Rule: The loaded robot returning to the scoring target maintains absolute right-of-way over the empty robot traveling to retrieve game elements. Emergency Contingency Protocols: In the event of partner disconnection or mechanical stall in the field corridor, the active robot immediately shifts to solo cycling without attempting hazardous pushes that could cause entanglement penalties.

title: Gracious Professionalism® & Coopertition® in the FIRST Ecosystem
description: Lending parts and technical support to rivals in the pits, mutual respect, and sportsmanship on the international stage.
body: In the FIRST Tech Challenge community, technical engineering and algorithmic mastery represent only half of the achievement metric. The remaining half is governed by two foundational philosophies originated by Dr. Woodie Flowers: Gracious Professionalism: Fierce competition combined with mutual respect, empathetic encouragement, and dignified demeanor under high stress. Coopertition: The principle that assisting competitors improves the entire tournament caliber without compromising one's own competitive potential. Every action inside the pit area and on the match field must reflect the six foundational pillars of FIRST: | Pillar | Practical Definition | Measurable Manifestation at Tournaments | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Discovery | Prioritizing intellectual growth over pure win/loss outcomes | Logging failed mechanisms and architectural pivots in the Engineering Portfolio | | Innovation | Applying creative problem solving to game constraints | Fabricating novel custom intake geometries instead of generic kit replicas | | Impact | Extending STEM skills to uplift surrounding communities | Hosting robotics workshops and mentoring rookie FIRST LEGO League teams | | Inclusion | Welcoming diverse perspectives, roles, and backgrounds | Ensuring all team members have dedicated speaking time in judging interviews | | Teamwork | Fostering mutual trust and cross-discipline collaboration | Clear operational boundaries between mechanical, electrical, and coding sub-teams | | Fun | Celebrating engineering, friendship, and festival atmosphere | Trading custom team pins, cheering for opposing alliances, and enjoying match play | The pit area serves as the true test environment for team culture. High-performing teams embody professional standards through actionable deeds: Spare Parts Dispatch: When a neighboring pit suffers a burned planetary gearbox, stripped spur gear, or broken REV Control Hub port, offer replacement hardware and tools without hesitation. Pit-side Technical Debugging: If a rookie squad struggles with Wi-Fi Direct channel conflicts or Robot Controller APK compilation errors, dispatch lead coders to guide them through network resets. Safety Culture as a Habit: Enforce ANSI Z87.1 approved safety glasses continuously upon entering the pit corridor. Keep workspace surfaces clear of loose aluminum shavings and pinched wiring. [Competitor Encountering Mechanical Failure] ──> [Proactive Assistance Offered] ──> [Shared Tools & Parts] │ ▼ [Both Robots Operational for Match] High-stakes competition inevitably produces tension—whether due to partner miscommunication, field disconnects, or unexpected referee penalties. Teams maintain poise through a disciplined resolution model: De-escalation: Decouple emotional frustration from technical facts. Never blame the student drive team for driver penalties or programmers for autonomous drift caused by floor seam bumps. Data-Driven Debriefs: Review recorded field telemetry logs and match footage to isolate root causes objectively (e.g., battery drop below 8.5V causing brownout resets). Graceful Referee Engagement: If a scoring rule needs clarification, only the designated Student Drive Team representative enters the referee Question Box, communicating respectfully with rule references.

title: Playoff Alliance Selection Dynamics: Secrets for Captains and Picks
description: 1-8 snake draft rules, strategic declines, compatibility between high-cycle scorers and defensive anchors.
body: Following the conclusion of the qualification matches, the top 4 ranked teams become Alliance Captains (Captains 1 through 4). Alliance Selection precedes the elimination bracket and directly determines tournament championship trajectories. Official FTC Alliance Selection adheres to strict tournament governance: Calling Order: Alliance Captain 1 calls first, followed in sequential order by Captains 2, 3, and 4. The Decline Rule: If Team B is invited by Alliance Captain A and declines the invitation, Team B is barred from being invited by any other alliance for the remainder of the draft. Team B may only continue in the tournament if they are ranked high enough to serve as an Alliance Captain themselves. The Slide-Up Dynamic: If a top-4 ranked team accepts an invitation from a higher-seeded alliance, the 5th-ranked team elevates to assume the role of Alliance Captain 4. Competitive teams never take the selection stage without an empirically ordered picklist ranked 1 through N based on scouting data. Selection criteria must focus on mechanical complementarity rather than nominal leaderboard rankings: | Strategic Vector | Weight | Evaluation Parameter | Elimination Objective | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Autonomous Compatibility | 30% | Coordinate collision risk and route flexibility | Simultaneous auto routines scoring maximum pre-loads without interference | | TeleOp Cycle Velocity | 35% | Normalized cycles completed per match | High sustained element throughput while withstanding opponent defensive pinning | | Endgame Rigging Reliability | 20% | Suspension cycle duration (sub-15 seconds) | Guaranteed endgame points executed cleanly before match clock expiration | | Defensive Resistance | 15% | Robot mass, traction wheel setup, low center of mass | Ability to hold field position against aggressive opposing defensive screening | When holding the Captain 1 seed, the conventional opening move is extending an invitation to Captain 2 to establish a dominant alliance. However, if Captain 2 declines to lead their own bracket or Captain 1 prefers a complementary specialist, an immediate contingency sequence activates: [Alliance Captain 1] │ Invite Captain 2? ─┼─ No (Select Highest Picklist Specialist) │ ┌─────────────────────┴─────────────────────┐ ▼ ▼ [Accepted] [Declined] ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────────────┐ │ Dominant Seed │ │ Captain 2 Locked Out │ │ Bracket Set │ │ Call Picklist Rank 1 │ └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────────────┘ Prior to the alliance selection ceremony, the Strategy Lead must conduct pit audits with prospective top-tier partners to verify three critical variables: Battery Health and Charge Status: Ensure the candidate possesses sufficient fresh packs exceeding 13.5V for rapid playoff turnaround. Drive Team Temperament: Confirm that the partner's drive team communicates cleanly and takes directional coaching during high-stress matches. Autonomous Script Flexibility: Verify that the partner has calibrated alternative autonomous variants (left/right starting positions, timed delays). Social Picking: Selecting familiar friend teams whose robots exhibit chronic Wi-Fi Direct disconnects or fragile mechanism linkages. Scoring Zone Chokepoints: Partnering with a robot that demands the exact same sub-field scoring space, causing gridlock during TeleOp cycling. Neglecting Opponent Counter-Play: Entering playoffs with lightweight, high-center-of-gravity builds that tip over under heavy field defense. Panic Calling on Decline: Freezing when a primary pick unexpectedly declines, resulting in an unvetted selection made under a ticking clock.

title: Comprehensive Breakdown of FTC Judged Awards
description: Deconstructing rubric expectations for the Inspire Award, Think, Innovate, Design, Connect, and Motivate accolades.
body: Awards in FIRST Tech Challenge evaluate far more than match scores. Judges look for technical rigor, team culture, community impact, and documented proof that design decisions drove real iteration. Seasonal rubrics evolve, so treat this breakdown as an engineering preparation model rather than an official rule substitute. Always consult current FIRST manuals before competition. The Inspire Award recognizes top-tier all-around teams. Winning submissions balance three parallel tracks: a competitive robot, transparent team operations, and sustained STEM outreach outside competition pits. Judges look for evidence showing how every member contributes, how knowledge transfers across seasons, and how outreach metrics reflect genuine change rather than one-off photo opportunities. | Assessment Area | Core Question Judges Ask | Concrete Evidence to Present | | --- | --- | --- | | Engineering | How did data guide your robot architecture? | CAD models, design logs, cycle time tests, stress plots | | Operations | How does the team manage resources and recruitment? | Skill matrices, team budget, onboarding schedule, retros | | Outreach | What measurable difference was made outside FTC? | Event logs, attendee demographics, partner testimonials | | Sustainability | Can this team repeat its success next season? | Multi-year funding plans, documentation handoffs, mentor logs | The Think Award honors teams who master iterative problem solving. Judges do not want a tidy after-the-fact narrative; they look for hypotheses, controlled bench tests, failure logs, and quantitative trade-off matrices. Showing why an intake or slide design failed—and how instrumented testing corrected the trajectory—proves technical maturity faster than unverified claims of perfection. Iterative Design Loop: [Problem Statement] -> [Design Hypotheses A/B/C] -> [CAD & Rapid Prototyping] ^ | | v [Design Adjustment] <-- [Bench Testing & Telemetry Log] <--+ Assign clear sub-system owners so every student speaks authoritatively on their contribution. Maintain a single shared terminology across portfolio, pit presentation, and notebook. Answer questions with a direct conclusion, then immediately offer primary evidence or test charts. Avoid memorized scripts that fall apart when judges probe edge cases. Treat every pit interaction as an extension of the formal interview room. Cross-check current season rubrics and flag pages matching each item. Audit all outreach numbers for verifiable dates, contact leads, and methodology. Ensure CAD renders show internal mechanisms, sensor mounts, and wire routing. Keep battery health logs and mechanical inspection sheets ready on pit tables.

title: Pit Station Management and the Vital Role of the Safety Captain
description: Organizing a 10x10ft pit garage, eye protection protocols, battery safety charging stations, and pre-match inspection checklists.
body: The pit area at a FIRST Tech Challenge tournament is a high-tempo workspace combining rapid hardware repairs, electrical debugging, battery rotation, and formal judge visits. Without structured management, pit congestion directly causes electrical shorts, lost tools, mechanical injuries, or missed queueing calls. The Safety Captain is not a decorative title; they hold field-level authority to enforce safety standards, control traffic, and guarantee operational readiness. The Safety Captain possesses stop-work authority whenever unsafe practices occur. Primary responsibilities include: Enforcing 100% compliance with ANSI Z87.1 safety glasses and closed-toe footwear for everyone entering the pit perimeter. Zoning pit space into repair benches, battery charging stations, software staging, and judge presentation areas. Maintaining the First Aid Kit and battery spill neutralizers (baking soda slurry or dry absorbent per applicable battery chemistry). Verifying and signing off on the pre-match technical checklist before the robot leaves for queueing. Briefing the team on venue emergency evacuation routes and nearest chemical extinguisher locations. Standard 12V competition batteries experience peak current draws between 20A and 30A during aggressive match cycles. Improper charging rates or degraded battery packs represent primary fire and brownout hazards. | Verification Item | Target Specification | Corrective Action When Out of Spec | | --- | --- | --- | | Open-circuit Voltage | \ge 13.0\textV at full charge | Relegate to slow equalization charge; retire packs below 12.0\textV | | Heat-shrink Wrap | Continuous, zero punctures, no swelling | Quarantine pack in fire-resistant LiPo/NiMH sack; label for disposal | | Power Connectors (XT30) | Tight mechanical retention, zero oxidation | Re-solder fresh connector with heat shrink before next match | | Operating Temperature | Below 40^\circ\textC during charge cycles | Immediately disconnect, vent pack, and mark out of match rotation | Standard FTC pit spaces span 3\textm \times 3\textm (or 10\textft \times 10\textft ). A functional spatial split prevents tool bottlenecks and keeps match preparation calm: +-------------------------------------------------------+ | [Judge Showcase & Portfolio] | [Main Pit Entrance] | | - Engineering documentation | - Visitor safety glasses| | - Autonomous telemetry kiosk | - Disinfectant & logs| +-------------------------------+-----------------------+ | [Hardware Workbench] | [Power & Battery Dock| | - Elevated robot stand | - Numbered battery bay| | - Hex keys, torque drivers | - Multi-channel smart charger| | - Debris & shaving bin | - Fireproof safe-box | +-------------------------------------------------------+ Before the drive team departs for the arena queue, the Safety Captain runs a strict five-point check: Mechanical Rigidity: Fastener torque check across chassis cross-members, chain and belt tension verified without tooth skip, thread-locker applied on high-vibration joints. Electrical Integrity: Main power XT30 harness locked to REV Control Hub, battery retained with dual Velcro straps, 20A main breaker operating cleanly without switch wiggle. Control Links: Driver Station confirms dual gamepads bound to port 1 and 2, 5GHz Wi-Fi ping under 15\textms , autonomous OpMode payload verified and ready. Bench Run Safety: Power cycle robot on an elevated stand to confirm wheel and intake spin direction prior to floor placement. Pit Discipline: Clear all walkways, stow precision measuring calipers, and ensure zero trailing extension cords across aisle boundaries.

title: Engineering Notebook vs Engineering Portfolio: Understanding the Evolution
description: The structural evolution from massive multi-binder notebooks to high-impact 15-page portfolios and digital archives.
body: In the FIRST Tech Challenge ecosystem, technical documentation serves as the direct communications conduit between your engineering lab and the judging panel. Rookie and intermediate teams frequently confuse the traditional long-form Engineering Notebook with the modern, page-constrained Engineering Portfolio. Differentiating both tools ensures balanced time allocation, prevents data loss, and directly optimizes award scoring. The Engineering Notebook is an unconstrained technical repository capturing the raw pulse of the season. Conversely, the Engineering Portfolio is a highly curated document (strictly capped at 15 content pages plus a cover page per FTC regulations) handed directly to tournament judges who evaluate technical, outreach, and business achievements in short review windows. | Evaluation Metric | Internal Engineering Notebook | Evaluated Engineering Portfolio | | --- | --- | --- | | Volume Ceiling | Unlimited ( 100 to 300+ pages) | Maximum 15 content pages + 1 cover page | | Primary Audience | Team members, mentors, future recruits | Competition judges ( 3 to 5 minute scan window) | | Content Nature | Chronological logs, raw failures, sensor logs | Curated milestones, trade-off matrices, clean graphs | | Primary Purpose | Long-term knowledge retention & handoff | Scoring rubric alignment for Inspire, Think, Connect | | Storage Format | Physical 3-ring binder or digital Notion wiki | High-resolution PDF printed and bound | Every square centimeter of the 15-page limit must deliver clear signal. A competition-proven layout allocates space proportionally across robot systems and organizational impact: Page 1: Team Identity & Strategic Overview: Team number, school affiliation, organizational hierarchy, season vision, core robot KPIs (weight, center of mass, cycle targets). Pages 2–8: Iterative Engineering Design Process: Problem breakdown, drivetrain architecture, intake subsystem, vertical extension/lift mechanics, and endgame mechanism. Include trade-off matrices, Finite Element Analysis (FEA) stress plots, and before-and-after photographic evidence. Pages 9–11: Software Architecture & Closed-Loop Controls: Sensor bus schematics, dead-wheel Odometry or AprilTag localization, feed-forward PIDF controller tuning charts, telemetry logs, and state machine architecture. Pages 12–14: Community Outreach & STEM Advocacy: Local school workshop series, FLL mentorship metrics, open-source library contributions, and quantitative impact assessments. Page 15: Financial Sustainability & Succession Planning: Annual budget balance sheet, corporate sponsors, grant acquisitions, and team knowledge-transfer pipelines. High-performing teams never draft their portfolio in a desperate rush during the final week before an event. Instead, run an automated weekly distillation pipeline: [Daily Lab Session / Raw Notebook Entries] | (Raw sensor drift measurements, sketch scans, CAD commits) v [Weekly Sprint Review / Retrospective] | (Filter key mechanical revisions, plot performance metrics) v [Portfolio Draft / 15-Page Canvas] (Trim prose, refine vector diagrams, verify minimum font size) Visual-to-Text Ratio: Aim for roughly 70% graphical elements (CAD screenshots, wiring schematics, cycle-time bar charts) and 30% concise technical narrative. Legibility Standards: Judges examine portfolios under variable pit and hotel lighting; never drop body typography below 9\textpt or condense line spacing unnaturally. Quantified Assertions: Replace vague descriptors such as "rapid intake" with verifiable metrics: "intakes four game elements in 2.8\texts with a zero-jam incident rate across 40 continuous bench runs."
